overview: Malaria is a life-threatening parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium parasites, transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It remains a major global health problem, especially in tropical and subtropical regions. Though preventable and treatable, malaria causes hundreds of millions of infections annually and is a leading cause of mortality in children under five.

types.name: Plasmodium falciparum Malaria
types.description: The most dangerous species, responsible for the majority of severe malaria cases and deaths. Causes cerebral malaria, severe anemia, and multi-organ failure.

types.name: Plasmodium vivax Malaria
types.description: Can remain dormant in the liver as hypnozoites and cause relapses months or years after initial infection. Common in Asia and Latin America.

types.name: Plasmodium ovale Malaria
types.description: Similar to P. vivax; milder disease with potential for relapse due to liver dormancy. Mainly found in West Africa.

types.name: Plasmodium malariae Malaria
types.description: Causes a mild, chronic infection. Can persist at low levels in blood for years if untreated. Associated with kidney disease in chronic cases.

types.name: Plasmodium knowlesi Malaria
types.description: A zoonotic species naturally infecting macaque monkeys. Can cause rapidly progressing severe disease in humans. Found in forested regions of Southeast Asia.

symptoms: Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes) due to red blood cell destruction
causes: Bite of infected female Anopheles mosquito injecting Plasmodium sporozoites
Congenital transmission from infected mother to newborn
Parasites invade liver cells then red blood cells, causing their rupture
risk_factors: Living in or travelling to malaria-endemic tropical regions (Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia)
Lack of mosquito net or repellent use
Outdoor exposure at night (when Anopheles mosquitoes are most active)
People with no prior immunity (first-time travellers to endemic areas)
Poor sanitation and stagnant water near homes
diagnosis: Microscopy of thick and thin blood smear — gold standard for species identification
Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs) — detect malaria antigens, fast results in field settings
PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) — highly sensitive, used in research and low-parasitemia cases
Complete blood count (CBC) — reveals anaemia and low platelets
Liver function tests and renal function tests in severe cases

uncomplicated_malaria: Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) — first-line treatment recommended by WHO
Artemether + Lumefantrine (Coartem) — most widely used ACT
Artesunate + Mefloquine — used in Southeast Asia
Chloroquine — only for P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae where resistant strains absent
severe_malaria: Intravenous (IV) Artesunate — first-line for severe malaria
Followed by full course of ACT after patient can take oral medication
IV Quinine + Doxycycline — alternative if artesunate unavailable
Supportive care: IV fluids, blood transfusion, oxygen, seizure management
radical_cure_relapse_prevention: Primaquine — to eliminate P. vivax and P. ovale dormant liver stages (hypnozoites)
G6PD testing required before Primaquine to avoid haemolysis in deficient patients
Tafenoquine — newer alternative to Primaquine for radical cure (single dose)
prevention_chemoprophylaxis: Doxycycline — for travellers to resistant areas

complications: Cerebral malaria — confusion, seizures, coma (mainly P. falciparum)
Acute kidney injury (blackwater fever — haemoglobin in urine)
Hypoglycaemia (especially in pregnant women and children)
prevention: Sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) every night
Indoor residual spraying (IRS) with approved insecticides
Use of insect repellents (DEET-based) on exposed skin
Wear long-sleeved clothing and long trousers at night
Malaria vaccination: RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) and R21/Matrix-M — for children in high-transmission areas
Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC) for children in Sahel region
Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp) using sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine
Eliminate standing water and mosquito breeding sites near homes
Take prescribed chemoprophylaxis before and during travel to endemic areas
emergency_signs: Altered consciousness, confusion, or coma (cerebral malaria)
Severe respiratory distress or laboured breathing
Inability to sit or stand (extreme weakness/prostration)
Passage of dark red/black urine (blackwater fever)
Heavy bleeding or signs of severe anaemia (extreme pallor)
Persistent vomiting — unable to take oral medication

faqs.question: Can malaria be completely cured?
faqs.answer: Yes, with correct treatment. P. falciparum malaria is curable with ACT. P. vivax and P. ovale require additional treatment with Primaquine to eliminate dormant liver stages and prevent relapse.

faqs.question: Can malaria relapse after treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes. P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) that can reactivate weeks to years later. Primaquine or Tafenoquine is required for radical cure and relapse prevention.

faqs.question: Is malaria contagious from person to person?
faqs.answer: Malaria cannot spread directly between people through casual contact. It is transmitted only via infected Anopheles mosquito bites. However, it can rarely spread through blood transfusion, organ transplant, or from mother to unborn child.

faqs.question: Is there a vaccine for malaria?
faqs.answer: Yes. RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) and R21/Matrix-M are WHO-recommended malaria vaccines for children in moderate-to-high transmission areas. They reduce severe malaria cases significantly but are not 100% protective — other preventive measures remain essential.
